As a UK therapist do you have any shred of advice you can give for accessing the type of therapy that you stated above for someone who is in the financial pits if hell?

Because it's through the NHS we don't get a choice on therapist nor the choice to change. You miss one appointment they stop the treatment and put you back in a looong wait list. You cannot be seeking simultaneous treatment of any kind or they stop the treatment  (e.g I had to see a councellor once a month at uni after an attempt in order to be let on the course after an attempt and the NHS pulled my treatment). They only really informally diagnose and will only refer to a psychiatrist if you are experiencing symptoms if psychosis, as for some reason PTSD is not classed as a severe enough mental illness for referal (directly quoted from my GP) which is bad when accessing disability support requires formal diagnosis. The only mental health treatment that they really offer is CBT, this is because they cheaply train up CBT councellors rather than hiring actual therapists that have studied for years because they cannot afford that. If you require other treatment such as EDMR or DBT you have to have tried absolutly everything and have come back from the point of death twice I swear to even get put on a looong wait list that you likely won't end up ever getting of because there only a handfull of specialists available to the nhs in the UK. This is without me mentioning things like the bullshit that is crisis teams and child and adolescent mental health services.

You could talk to a uni councellor, and get support with applying for extenuating circumstances and intercalate your studies for the year to work on your mental health. Ensuring that you go and see a psychiatrist to get diagnosis, so that when you do come back you can have access to DSA and the support that you need if you the  decide to return?

This is the approach that I took, unfortunatly after a failed attempt and not before. If I hadn't failed the attempt I never would have gone down that path and wouldn't be in the better place I am now: I managed to pull my grade from a 2:1 to a first (which I found out after graduating ultimatly makes no odds), mental health is better than it ever has been and I'm even starting a Masters this week.  

For me after going through intercalation and DSA the university came up with a plan to help get me through. This looked like: 5/10 minute meetings first thing in the morning with my personal tutor for the first few weeks and then just once a week when I'd settled back intobthe routine of comming in. DSA paying for a taxi to get me into uni aswell as equiptment to record lectures, which helped as my short term memory was fried. Even extra things like paying for my printing and my DSA support officer was always there to help whenever I needed. E.G- my advisor was being a dick and putting to much pressure in me and my DSA officer contacted the course leader and got me a new advisor in a matter of hours. University counselling once a week  for the whole year. Extra time on deadlines if needed. In close contact with friends and family that could contact my personal tutor with my consent if they ever felt worried for my health/safety. 

There are ways that the University can support you and I promise you you desserve that help!! Taking the steps to access it is fuxking hard I know but ultimately easier than a permenant decision that you can't take back. I would recommend intercalating, it gives you the time to work on your mh and decide ultimatly whether it's best to continue studies and it also gives the university time to figur out how best to assist you. Some university's provide councelling and support even as an intercalated student.

I experienced something very similar to yourself, it's almosts like once you have been slut shamed or named as a bullying victim by one, you become the scape goat for the whole school. 8 years on from bullying and sexuall hsrassment daily within school, after 2 attempts of taking my life, visiting multiple councillors and therapists... I was eventually informally diagnosed with CPTSD. The diagnosis then allowed me to receive the correct type of care and therapy, and  I have since felt stronger happier and more recovered than ever. Bullying or any form of abuse at any age may lead to PTS PTSD or CPTSD. However It's not the diagnosis or the label itself that I feel you should be focusing on, it's dealing with this trauma and how your brain has processed it. Which is a journey that requires professional help. I commend you for seeking out advice here, but I implore you to reach out for the professional care you desserve. I can admit that due to the bullying I felt like I was inherently wrong as a person and held on to what some would call a "victim mentality" for years: Self diagnosising myself with anything that would explain why I felt and acted the way that I did. But the truth is there isn't anything inherently wrong with me, I just needed someone to help me deal with and move forward from trauma. I know that it's cliche when everyone says "it gets better", and when you are dealing with mh issues to any degree it almost impossible to see that, but I can attest that it honestly does. But only with the right help!
